title: How Fast Does a New Virus Spread? Reading the First Weeks of COVID-19 in Wuhan

source.title: Early Transmission Dynamics in Wuhan, China, of Novel Coronavirus–Infected Pneumonia

intro.summary: The paper asks how a brand-new coronavirus behaved in its first weeks in Wuhan: how long people took to fall ill after infection, how fast cases grew, and how many people each patient infected. The authors studied the first 425 laboratory-confirmed cases. They fitted simple probability curves to the timing data and a transmission model to the early growth in cases. They found a mean incubation period of 5.2 days, with 95% of people ill by 12.5 days. Early on, cases doubled every 7.4 days, and each case led to about 2.2 others (R0, with a wide range of 1.4 to 3.9). The main limits are small samples: incubation came from 10 cases and the serial interval from 6 pairs. A prior borrowed from SARS shaped the estimate, and mild or unusual cases were likely missed. This lesson does not cover super-spreading, control measures in detail, or how testing changes over time affect estimates; those make good follow-up topics.
background: Epidemiology is the study of how diseases spread through populations, much as a traffic engineer studies how jams spread along roads.
A virus is a tiny germ that can only multiply inside living cells; a coronavirus is one family of viruses, which includes the ones behind SARS and some common colds.
Pneumonia is an infection that inflames the lungs, and it was the illness doctors first noticed in Wuhan.
A 95% confidence interval is a range of plausible values for a number estimated from limited data: the wider the range, the less sure the estimate.
intro.aha: From just two timing facts, that cases doubled every 7.4 days and that each new patient fell ill about 7.5 days after the one who infected them, you can work out that each patient infected about 2.2 other people, without ever watching a single infection happen.

primer.heading: The question
primer.body: In December 2019, doctors in Wuhan, China, began seeing pneumonia cases from an unknown cause. The cause turned out to be a new coronavirus, later named SARS-CoV-2. Nobody yet knew how it spread or how fast. Health officials needed numbers fast: how long people stay healthy after catching it, how quickly cases grow, and how many people each patient infects.
primer.quote: Here, we provide an analysis of data on the first 425 laboratory-confirmed cases in Wuhan to describe the epidemiologic characteristics and transmission dynamics of NCIP.

primer.heading: What they did
primer.body: Field teams interviewed patients, relatives and contacts. They recorded when each person fell ill, whom they had been near, and when they saw a doctor. From these dates the authors fitted smooth curves describing typical delays, such as the time from catching the virus to feeling sick. They then used the early rise in cases, up to January 4, to estimate how fast the outbreak was growing and how many people each case infected.

primer.heading: What they found
primer.body: Most people fell ill about 5 days after infection, but a few took much longer. Cases doubled roughly every week. Each patient passed the virus to about 2.2 others on average. Because that number is above 1, the outbreak would keep growing unless something changed. Early cases were tied to a seafood market, but later ones were not, which showed that people were infecting each other.
primer.quote: The mean incubation period was 5.2 days (95% confidence interval [CI], 4.1 to 7.0), with the 95th percentile of the distribution at 12.5 days. In its early stages, the epidemic doubled in size every 7.4 days.

primer.heading: Why it matters, and its limits
primer.body: These numbers backed a 14-day quarantine and showed that strong efforts would be needed to stop the spread. They also became starting points for later forecasts around the world. The estimates rest on very few cases, though, and the plausible ranges are wide: R0 could have been anywhere from 1.4 to 3.9. Mild cases were probably missed, and testing improved over time, which can distort growth estimates.
primer.quote: Our estimate was based on information from 10 cases and is somewhat imprecise; it would be important for further studies to provide more information on this distribution.

concepts.title: Doubling: how a steady growth rate sets a fixed doubling time
concepts.idea: When cases grow by the same percentage each day, they double over a fixed number of days, and a faster daily growth rate means a shorter doubling time.

predict.question: An outbreak has been doubling every 7 days. Control measures then cut its daily growth rate to one third of what it was. If the new rate holds steady, how long does each doubling now take?
options: About 21 days
About 2.3 days
About 10 days
Still 7 days
why: Right: doubling time is ln 2 divided by the growth rate. Cut the rate to a third and the wait to double becomes three times longer: 3 × 7 = 21 days.
This divides 7 by 3, as if a slower rate gave quicker doubling. It works the other way: a slower rate means a longer wait for each doubling.
This guesses that the wait grows a little but not in step. Doubling time is inversely proportional to the rate, so a third of the rate means exactly three times the wait.
The doubling time is fixed only while the rate stays the same. Once the rate changes, the doubling time changes with it.

terms.means: Growth by the same percentage each day, so the count keeps doubling at a steady pace
The number of days it takes for the case count to double
How fast cases rise per day, as a share of the current count. A rate of 0.10 means roughly 10% more cases each day

model.title: Cases over 40 days in a steadily spreading outbreak
model.note: Teaching model: cases rise smoothly by the same percentage every day. There are no reporting delays, no chance ups and downs, and no running out of people to infect. The curve uses r as a continuous rate, so the extra cases per day equal e^r − 1, slightly more than r itself. Numbers are illustrative, not the paper's data. The walkthrough states clearly when it quotes the paper's own estimates.

steps.say: This curve counts the cases in a made-up outbreak, day by day, over 40 days.
This slider sets how fast the count rises each day. Watch the curve bend upward more steeply.
This slider sets how many cases there are on day 0, where the curve starts.
These lines mark the days when the count reaches 2, 4 and 8 times its starting size.
This box shows how many days the count takes to double. Keep an eye on it.

explore.prompt: Now play with it. Make the outbreak speed up, then reach a large count from a tiny start.

goals.text: Make the cases double twice as fast as they do at the start
hints: Doubling twice as fast means the wait to double has to be cut in half.
Watch the 'Days for cases to double' box while you move the speed slider.
Remember what happened in the walkthrough when the speed itself was doubled.

goals.text: Start from a single case and still pass 80 cases by day 30
hints: Going from 1 case to 80 takes a little over six doublings (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128).
All of those doublings must fit inside 30 days, so each one has to be quick.
You need a doubling time a bit under 5 days. Nudge the speed slider up until the day-30 box passes 80.

feedback.correct: Yes. Doubling time equals ln 2 divided by the growth rate. One third of the rate means three times the wait: about 21 days per doubling instead of 7.
feedback.incorrect: A slower growth rate does not shorten the doubling time or leave it unchanged. Doubling time is inversely proportional to the rate. Cut the rate to a third and each doubling takes three times as long, about 21 days.

steps.say: Start slow. The count rises about 5% a day, and going from 5 cases to 10 takes about 14 days.
Compare the gaps between the lines. Going from 5 to 10 takes about 14 days, and 10 to 20 takes another 14. Each doubling takes the same wait. That wait is the doubling time.

Why the same wait? Each day adds the same percentage, not the same number of people. Bigger counts add more people per day, so the count always needs the same time to double. This is called exponential growth.
Now start from 15 cases instead of 5. The curve sits higher, but the doubling time does not budge. It depends only on the speed.
The speed slider is the growth rate. Double it from 0.05 to 0.10 per day. The doubling time halves, to about 7 days.
Early in Wuhan, the paper estimated a rate of 0.10 per day and a doubling time of 7.4 days. That rate is rounded: a doubling time of exactly 7.4 days matches a rate of about 0.094.
Double the rate again, to 0.20 per day. Now cases double every 3.5 days, and the curve shoots off the top of the chart within weeks.

understand.explanation: When cases grow by the same percentage every day, the count doubles over a fixed number of days. This happens whatever the starting number. That fixed wait is the doubling time, and it equals ln 2 (about 0.69) divided by the daily growth rate. So doubling the growth rate halves the doubling time. The paper fitted a transmission model to Wuhan cases that fell ill between December 10 and January 4. It estimated a growth rate of 0.10 per day and a doubling time of 7.4 days. Both estimates are uncertain: the 95% confidence interval for doubling runs from 4.2 to 14 days. The authors also stopped at January 4 on purpose, because more testing after that would make cases seem to grow faster than they really did.
understand.quote: In the epidemic curve up to January 4, 2020, the epidemic growth rate was 0.10 per day (95% CI, 0.050 to 0.16) and the doubling time was 7.4 days (95% CI, 4.2 to 14).

connect.caption: The paper reports both a growth rate r (0.10 per day) and a doubling time (7.4 days), but it does not print the formula that links them. This is the standard rule our model uses. The orange part is the speed slider r, and the coloured result is the 'Days for cases to double' box. ln 2 ≈ 0.69, so a rate of 0.10 gives about 6.9 days. The paper's 7.4 days reflects its unrounded rate.

concepts.recap: A steady daily growth rate means a fixed doubling time of about 0.69 ÷ rate: double the rate and each doubling takes half as long.

concepts.title: Incubation is a spread, not one number: why quarantine is 14 days
concepts.idea: The time from infection to illness varies from person to person, so a quarantine must be long enough to cover the slow tail of the distribution, not just the average.

predict.question: Two new viruses both make people wait 5 days on average before they feel ill. With Virus A, almost everyone falls ill between day 4 and day 6. With Virus B, some fall ill on day 1 and a few not until day 15. Which virus needs the longer quarantine to catch 95 in 100 cases?
options: Virus A, because its cases bunch tightly around day 5
Virus B, because its slowest cases come much later
Both need the same length, because their averages are the same
why: Bunching sounds 'busier', but a tight bunch means almost no one is still waiting after day 6, so a short quarantine already catches nearly everyone.
Right: the quarantine has to reach past the slow tail, and Virus B's tail stretches to about day 15, so it needs a much longer quarantine than Virus A.
It is tempting to plan around the average, but the average says nothing about the slowest people. Equal averages can hide very different tails, as the spread slider showed.

terms.means: The time from catching an infection to first feeling ill
How a quantity is spread out across people: how many have each possible value
The stretched-out side of a lopsided curve, where a few people have much larger values than most
The value that 95 in 100 people are at or below; only 5 in 100 go beyond it

model.title: How many days until people who caught the virus feel ill
model.note: Teaching model: a smooth lopsided (log-normal) curve, the shape the paper fitted, with its average fixed at the paper's 5.2 days. At the default spread, 95 in 100 people are ill by about 12.5 days, matching the paper. The paper's estimate came from only 10 cases and is uncertain (the 95-in-100 day has a 95% CI of 9.2 to 18 days). Other spread settings are illustrative, not the paper's data.

outputs.label: Of 1,000 people, fall ill after release

y.label: Share first feeling ill that day

series.label: When people first feel ill
series.expr: exp(-((ln(max(x, 0.01)) - ln(5.2) + spread^2 / 2)^2) / (2 * spread^2)) / (max(x, 0.01) * spread * sqrt(2 * pi))

steps.say: Picture a crowd who all caught the virus on day 0. The height of this hump shows how many first feel ill on each day after that.
This line marks 5.2 days: the average wait before feeling ill.
This slider sets how long exposed people stay in quarantine. Green: fell ill while still inside. Orange: fell ill after going home.
This slider changes how much people differ from each other. The average stays at 5.2 days the whole time.
These two boxes count who is caught in time and who slips out.

explore.prompt: Now you set the quarantine. Drag it, change how much people differ, and watch the orange tail.

goals.text: Find a quarantine just long enough to catch at least 95 in 100 people before release, and no longer than needed.
hints: Which part of the curve decides how many slip out: the tall hump or the thin right-hand tail?
Drag the quarantine slider right, well past the average line, and watch the green box climb.
The green box crosses 95% somewhere between 12 and 14 days.

goals.text: Keep a 14-day quarantine, but make people differ enough that more than 5 in 100 would fall ill after release. The average stays 5.2 days.
hints: What could stretch the tail further right without moving the average?
Set the quarantine to 14 days, then drag the 'How much people differ' slider to the right.
You won't need to go all the way to the right end of that slider.

feedback.correct: Yes. A quarantine is judged by the slowest people, not the typical one. Virus B's long tail reaches about day 15, so it needs a far longer quarantine than Virus A, even though both averages are 5 days.
feedback.incorrect: You may have planned around the average or the busiest days. But people released before they fall ill are the ones in the slow tail. Two viruses with the same average can have very different tails, and the longer tail needs the longer quarantine.

steps.say: Start with a quarantine of 5 days, close to the 5.2-day average. This wait from catching the virus to feeling ill is called the incubation period.
Look at the boxes: only about 6 in 10 fall ill in time. About 390 of every 1,000 would fall ill after going home.
Why so many? Because the wait is not the same for everyone. How the waits spread across the days is called a distribution, and this curve is it.
The curve is lopsided. It rises fast, then trails off slowly to the right. That stretched right side is the long tail. Even at 9 days, about 1 in 8 people are still waiting.
At about 12.5 days, 95 in 100 people have fallen ill. That day is the 95th percentile. The paper estimated it at 12.5 days, using 10 cases.
A 14-day quarantine goes a little further, which gives a safety margin. About 965 in 1,000 are now caught, but roughly 35 still slip out.
Now make people differ less, with the same 5.2-day average. The tail shrinks and 14 days catches almost everyone. The tail, not the average, sets the length.
Back at the paper's spread, compare the two lines. A quarantine at the average lets about 4 in 10 out early. Fourteen days reaches past nearly all of the tail.

understand.explanation: People who catch the virus do not all fall ill after the same number of days. Their waits form a lopsided curve: most fall ill within a few days, but a long tail of people take up to two weeks. A quarantine set at the average (5.2 days) would release about 4 in 10 infected people before they felt ill, so its length has to reach into that tail. The paper fitted a curve to the exposure and illness dates of 10 cases. It found a mean of 5.2 days (95% CI, 4.1 to 7.0) and a 95th percentile of 12.5 days (95% CI, 9.2 to 18). This supports a 14-day quarantine. With only 10 cases the authors call the estimate 'somewhat imprecise': the true 95-in-100 day could be as late as 18 days, and even 14 days does not catch absolutely everyone.
understand.quote: Our preliminary estimate of the incubation period distribution provides important evidence to support a 14-day medical observation period or quarantine for exposed persons.

connect.caption: This is the model's rule, not an equation printed in the paper. The paper says it fitted a log-normal curve to the incubation data, and this is the share of a log-normal that falls before day q. Orange q is the quarantine length slider. Purple σ is 'How much people differ'. Green is the 'Fall ill during quarantine' box. Fixing μ this way keeps the average at the paper's 5.2 days, so a larger σ stretches the tail without moving the average.

concepts.recap: The wait before illness varies from person to person. A quarantine must outlast the slow tail (about 12.5 days for 95 in 100 here), not the 5.2-day average, which is why 14 days was supported.

concepts.title: The fake dip: why the newest days always look quiet
concepts.idea: Because cases are counted by the day people fell ill but take days to be reported, an epidemic that is still growing appears to fall off in its most recent days.

predict.question: A different city plots its cases by the day symptoms started. In today's data, the last 6 days drop sharply. There, it usually takes about 9 days before a sick person shows up in the data. What is the best reading of the drop?
options: The outbreak has probably turned a corner and is now shrinking
A 9-day lag would produce a drop like this even if cases were still rising, so the drop alone can't tell us yet
Cases must still be rising, because a drop at the end of the data is always fake
why: A falling line looks like good news. But with a 9-day lag, most people who fell ill in the last 6 days haven't been counted yet, so a growing epidemic would look just like this.

Right. A lag this long hides most of the newest cases, so a rising epidemic and a slowing one can look the same here. You need to wait for those days to fill in, or correct for the lag, before judging the trend.
It is tempting after seeing the model, but the lag only means the drop can't be trusted. A real slowdown is also possible. The recent days simply can't tell the two apart yet.

terms.means: The day a person's symptoms began
A chart of how many people fell ill on each day, plotted by onset date
The time between a person falling ill and their case appearing in the data
Cases that really exist but have not been found or counted yet

model.title: Real new cases vs. cases counted so far, by the day people fell ill
model.note: Teaching model: real cases grow by a fixed share each day, and each person's wait before being counted is random, with the stated average (an exponential spread, so many are counted fast and a few take very long). Only the lag is modelled. Changes in testing, case definitions and true slowdowns are left out. The default growth of 10% a day is the paper's early Wuhan estimate (0.10 per day). The lag values and curve heights are illustrative, not the paper's data.

controls.label: Average days from falling ill to being counted

outputs.label: Counted line seems to peak (days before data pulled)
Last week's real cases not yet counted
outputs.expr: ((1 - exp(-7 * (growth + 1 / delay))) / (growth + 1 / delay)) / ((1 - exp(-7 * growth)) / growth)

x.label: Day people fell ill (day 40 = day the data were pulled)

y.label: People per day (real count on day 40 = 100)

steps.say: Each spot along the bottom is a day. On day 40, at the right edge, someone pulls the data and draws this chart.
The dashed line is how many people really fell ill each day. It climbs right up to the edge.
The solid line is what the chart actually shows: only the people who had been counted by day 40.
This slider sets how many days, on average, pass between someone falling ill and being counted. Watch the solid line sag.
This one sets how fast real cases grow each day.
These numbers show where the solid line seems to top out, and how much of last week is still missing.

explore.prompt: Play with the counting lag and the growth speed, and make the fake decline as convincing as you can.

goals.text: Keep growth at 10% a day and find the shortest average lag that hides more than half of last week's real cases
hints: Which slider controls how long people wait before they are counted?
Watch the 'not yet counted' number as you lengthen the lag one day at a time. Stop as soon as it passes 50%.
It crosses 50% between the default lag and a week. Try the days just above the default.

goals.text: Make the solid line seem to peak at least 10 days before the data were pulled
hints: A longer lag pushes the fake peak back, but even the longest lag isn't enough at the default growth.
Think about the other slider: when real cases climb more slowly, the newest days aren't much bigger than older ones, so the lag wins over a longer stretch.
Max out the lag, then lower the growth step by step until the peak sits 10 or more days back. Halfway to the minimum is enough.

feedback.correct: Yes. With a 9-day lag, most people who fell ill in the last 6 days are still uncounted, so a rising epidemic would show the same drop. The recent days can't be read yet.
feedback.incorrect: The drop sits exactly where a long lag hides cases, so it can't tell a real slowdown from a fake one. It neither shows the outbreak is easing nor proves it is still growing. Wait for those days to fill in, or correct for the lag.

steps.say: Start with a fast count: people are counted about a day after falling ill, and real cases grow 10% a day, the pace the paper found early in Wuhan. The two lines almost match. Only the last couple of days sag.

Each person sits on the day their symptoms began, their onset date. Counting people by onset date gives the epidemic curve. Both lines here are epidemic curves: the real one and the one known on day 40.
The wait between falling ill and being counted is the reporting delay. Make it 3 days on average: a bump appears, and the counted line now seems to peak about 4 days before the edge.
Stretch the delay to a week. The fake peak slides further back and the drop deepens. About two-thirds of last week's real cases haven't been counted yet.
Those cases are real but not yet found. Epidemiologists call this under-ascertainment. Look at the shaded last week: the dashed line keeps rising there while the solid line falls.
Now slow the real growth to 5% a day. The fake peak moves even further back, because the newest days are no longer much bigger than the days before, so the missing cases weigh more.

Wuhan-like numbers: 10% growth and a 10-day lag (admission took 9 to 12.5 days on average there). Real cases never stop climbing, yet the chart seems to peak a week ago, with three-quarters of last week missing.

understand.explanation: Each case is placed on the day its symptoms began, but it only enters the data after the person sees a doctor, gets tested and is reported. So on the day the data are pulled, the newest days hold only the few people who were counted fast. The curve then sags at the end even while real cases are still climbing. The longer the delay, the deeper this fake dip and the further back the fake peak. The Wuhan team saw just such a decline at the end of their curve and judged it an artefact of delayed reporting, not a turning point. To estimate growth, they used only people who fell ill up to January 4. One caveat pulls the other way: testing kits became more available during January, so part of the later rise may reflect more testing rather than more infections.
understand.quote: The development of the epidemic follows an exponential growth in cases, and a decline in the most recent days is likely to be due to under-ascertainment of cases with recent onset and delayed identification and reporting rather than a true turning point in incidence

check.task: Real cases grow at 15% a day or faster, yet make the counted line seem to peak at least 5 days before the data were pulled.
check.hint: Fast growth pulls the fake peak toward the edge, so you need the other slider to push it back. How long must people wait before being counted?
check.misconception: That a fast-growing epidemic can't look like it is falling, so only slow outbreaks show a fake dip. In fact, any epidemic can, as long as the reporting delay is long enough.

connect.caption: This is the teaching model's rule, not an equation from the paper. Real cases grow at rate r (the growth slider). The bracket is the share of people who fell ill on that day and have already been counted when the average lag is D (the delay slider). That share falls to zero on the newest day, which creates the dip. Setting the slope to zero gives the fake peak. The paper itself corrected for this lag by only using onsets up to January 4 when estimating growth.

concepts.recap: When cases are plotted by the day people fell ill, the newest days are always undercounted, so a falling tail in fresh data is not evidence that an epidemic is slowing.

concepts.title: The serial interval: the gap between one patient and the next
concepts.idea: The serial interval is the time from one person falling ill to the person they infected falling ill, and it sets how often a new 'generation' of cases appears.

predict.question: Two made-up outbreaks start on the same day, and in each every sick person infects the same number of people. In A, the average gap from one person falling ill to the next is 5 days. In B it is 10 days. After 30 days, which has gone through more rounds?
options: Outbreak A, the one with the 5-day gap
Outbreak B, the one with the 10-day gap
Both the same, because each person infects the same number of people
You can't tell without knowing the incubation period
why: Right: 30 ÷ 5 gives about 6 rounds, while 30 ÷ 10 gives only about 3. A shorter gap means each new round of cases arrives sooner.
A longer gap might sound like more time to spread, but it means each round takes longer to arrive, so fewer rounds fit into 30 days.
The number infected per person sets how big each round is. The gap sets how often a new round comes, and here the gaps differ.
The incubation period is a different delay, from catching the virus to falling ill. The pace of rounds comes from the illness-to-illness gap, which is given here.

terms.means: The number of days from one person falling ill to the person they infected falling ill
One round of cases: the people infected by the round before them
A lopsided curve often used for waiting times: it never goes below zero and has a long tail of slow cases
A small group of cases linked by contact, such as people in one household

model.title: Days from one person falling ill to the next person falling ill
model.note: Teaching model: each curve is a gamma distribution set by its average and spread. This is the same family of curve the paper fitted, and the model computes it with a close approximation. 'Rounds in 30 days' simply divides 30 by the average gap and ignores overlap between rounds. The dashed curve (average 7.5 days, spread 3.4) and the range markers at 5.3 and 19 days (the 95% confidence interval for the average) are the paper's estimates from 6 pairs of cases. All other settings are illustrative.

outputs.label: Most common gap
outputs.expr: m >= sd ? m - sd * sd / m : 0

x.label: Days between one person falling ill and the next

markers.x: m >= sd ? m - sd * sd / m : 0
markers.label: Peak

steps.say: This curve shows how many days pass from one sick person falling ill to the person they passed it to falling ill. Taller means more common.
This slider sets the average gap. Watch the whole curve slide to the right.
This one sets how much the gap varies from one pair of people to another.
This switch adds the paper's own estimate as a dashed curve, so you can compare.
And this box counts how many rounds of passing it on fit into 30 days.

explore.prompt: Play with the gap between one person falling ill and the next. Change how fast new rounds of cases arrive, then change the shape of the curve without moving its average.

goals.text: Make a new round of illness come along five times in 30 days.
hints: Do shorter gaps or longer gaps fit more rounds into a month?
The rounds box is just 30 divided by the average gap.
You need an average a little shorter than the paper's 7.5 days.

goals.text: Keep the average gap at the paper's 7.5 days, but make the most common gap fall below 5 days.
hints: Which slider changes the curve's shape without moving its average?
Widen the spread and watch the Peak line move while the Average line stays put.
The peak slides left as the spread grows. You need a spread well above the paper's.

feedback.correct: Yes. How often a new round of cases appears depends on the average serial interval: 30 ÷ 5 gives about 6 generations in a month, but 30 ÷ 10 gives only about 3.
feedback.incorrect: The number of people each case infects sets how big each round is. The serial interval sets how often a round comes. A shorter average gap means generations arrive faster, so outbreak A goes through about 6 rounds to B's 3.

steps.say: Here is the paper's estimate. Each point on the curve is a possible number of days between one patient falling ill and the person they infected falling ill. This gap is called the serial interval.
On average the gap is 7.5 days. Some pairs fall ill only a few days apart, and others two weeks or more.

The curve is lopsided: a gap can't be shorter than zero, but it can be very long. The paper used this kind of curve, a gamma distribution. So the most common gap, about 6 days, sits left of the average.
Each step along a chain is one generation: the people infected by the round before. With 7.5-day gaps, about 4 generations fit into 30 days.
Shrink the average gap to 5 days. Now a new generation arrives about 6 times a month. The outbreak takes its steps faster.
Stretch it to 15 days and only 2 generations fit into a month. Same virus chains, slower rhythm.

How sure is the paper? A cluster is a small group of cases linked by contact, like one household. The estimate came from just 6 pairs of cases in 5 such clusters, and its likely range for the average runs from 5.3 days all the way to 19.
If the true average were near the top of that range, the curve would sit far to the right of the dashed estimate, with fewer than 2 generations a month. Six pairs can't rule that out.

understand.explanation: When one sick person infects another, the second person falls ill some days later. The serial interval is that gap, measured from the first person's illness to the second person's illness. Illness dates are easy to record, while the moment of infection usually isn't. The gap differs from pair to pair, so it is a lopsided curve rather than one number, and its average sets how often a new generation of cases appears. The paper used illness dates from 6 pairs of linked cases, each pair from a cluster of cases known to be in contact, and fitted a gamma curve with an average of 7.5 days. With so few pairs the estimate is rough: the average could plausibly be anywhere from 5.3 to 19 days.
understand.quote: On the basis of the dates of illness onset of 6 pairs of cases in these clusters, we estimated that the serial interval distribution had a mean (±SD) of 7.5±3.4 days (95% CI, 5.3 to 19) (Figure 2B).

connect.caption: The paper fitted a gamma distribution to the serial interval but does not print a formula, so this is the model's rule. The blue average-gap slider is the mean serial interval (7.5 days in the paper), the orange spread slider is its SD (3.4 days), and dividing 30 days by the mean gives the rough number of generations per month shown in the rounds box.

concepts.recap: The serial interval is the gap from one case's illness to the illness of the case it caused; its average sets how often new generations appear.

activities.title: A made-up family chain

steps.text: Day 0: Dad, who shops at a busy market, falls ill.
Day 7: his daughter falls ill. She met no other sick people, so he must have infected her.
Day 15: her little brother falls ill after she looked after him at home.
Nobody knows the exact moment each child caught the virus. But everyone remembers the day each one fell ill, so the gaps can still be measured.
Two gaps of 7 and 8 days average 7.5 days. But with only two pairs, the next family might easily show a gap of 4 days or 12.
steps.result: Few pairs means a rough average

activities.takeaway: The serial interval links illness dates along a chain. Each gap is one step from a case to the case it caused, and each step is a new generation.

activities.title: Which delay is it?
activities.prompt: Sort each delay. Mia and the nurse are made up; the averages quoted are the paper's.

groups.label: Incubation period: catching it → falling ill yourself
Serial interval: one person falling ill → the person they infected falling ill

cards.text: Mia caught the virus at a dinner on Monday and felt sick on Saturday.
cards.feedback: It runs from the moment of infection to Mia's own illness, all within one person. That is incubation.

cards.text: Mia felt sick on Saturday. Her husband, whom she infected, felt sick 6 days later.
cards.feedback: It runs from one person's illness to the illness of the person they infected. That is the serial interval.

cards.text: A nurse treated a patient without protection on the 3rd and fell ill on the 8th.
cards.feedback: Tricky: two people are involved, but the gap starts when the nurse was infected, not when the patient fell ill. So it is the nurse's incubation.

cards.text: The paper's average of 5.2 days, from exposure histories of 10 cases.
cards.feedback: Exposure to illness onset in the same person: this is the paper's incubation estimate.

cards.text: The paper's average of 7.5 days, from the illness dates of 6 pairs of cases.
cards.feedback: Illness date to illness date across pairs: this is the paper's serial interval estimate.

cards.text: Mia felt sick on Saturday and first saw a doctor on Tuesday.
cards.feedback: This is the onset-to-first-medical-visit delay. The paper measured it too, but it says nothing about passing the virus on.

cards.text: Patients falling ill between January 1 and 11 waited 9.1 days on average from illness to hospital admission.
cards.feedback: Onset to admission is about care, not transmission, so it is neither of the two.

activities.takeaway: Incubation happens inside one person, from infection to illness. The serial interval spans two people, from one illness to the next, and that is what sets the pace of new generations.

concepts.title: R0 and the tipping point at 1
concepts.idea: R0 is the average number of people one case infects in a population with no immunity; if it is above 1 each generation is bigger than the last, and if it is below 1 the outbreak shrinks.

predict.question: The paper notes that SARS had an R0 of about 3 and was brought under control by isolating patients. In this simple model, roughly what share of infections would isolation need to block to make a SARS outbreak shrink?
options: About a third
About half
More than two-thirds
All of them
why: A third sounds like a lot, but 3 × (1 − 1/3) = 2. Each case still infects two people, so every generation is double the last.
Blocking half works when each case would infect about 2. Here 3 × 0.5 = 1.5, which is still above 1, so the outbreak keeps growing.
Correct. For 3 × (share left) to fall below 1, the share left must be under one-third. That means more than two-thirds of infections must be blocked.
Perfection isn't needed. Once each case infects fewer than one other person on average, every generation is smaller than the last and the outbreak fades, even though some spread still happens.

terms.means: The average number of people one case infects when nobody in the population is immune yet, said 'R-nought'.
The tipping point at 1 infection per case: above it an outbreak grows, below it the outbreak shrinks.

model.title: How big each generation of cases gets
model.note: Teaching model: every case infects exactly the average number of people. Nobody becomes immune, so the pool of people who can catch the virus never runs out. Control measures remove a fixed share of infections. The model starts from 100 cases. The default of 2.2 is the paper's estimate for Wuhan up to January 4; all other numbers are illustrative, not the paper's data.

steps.say: Each bar is one generation of cases: the people infected by the bar before it. The first bar holds 100 sick people.
This slider sets how many people each sick person passes the virus to when nothing is done to stop it.
This slider sets the share of those infections that control measures, such as isolating patients, manage to block.
These boxes show how many people each case really infects, and how big the sixth generation ends up.
Watch the bars as the first slider moves up.

explore.prompt: Now steer the outbreak yourself. Use the two sliders to make the generations grow, hold steady or fade.

goals.text: Keep each case infecting 2.2 people unchecked, as the paper estimated, and use control measures alone to make the outbreak shrink.
hints: What must the 'actually infects' number fall below for each bar to be smaller than the one before?
Blocking a share of infections multiplies 2.2 by the share that is left. You need 2.2 × (share left) to come out below 1.
Blocking half is not quite enough. Go a little further and watch the last bar.

goals.text: Switch on some control measures and make the outbreak hold perfectly steady, with generation 6 the same size as generation 1.
hints: Steady means each case replaces itself exactly once, no more and no less.
Choose an unchecked spread first. Then block just enough that the share left, times that spread, equals 1.
If each case would infect two people unchecked, what share must be blocked to leave exactly one?

feedback.correct: Right. With an R0 of about 3, each case must be left infecting fewer than one person, so the share of infections still getting through must be under a third. That means blocking more than two-thirds. The higher R0 is, the more control it takes to cross the tipping point.
feedback.incorrect: The goal is not to block 'a lot' but to push the number each case actually infects below 1. With an R0 of 3, that means blocking more than two-thirds of infections. Blocking less only slows the growth; blocking all of them isn't required.

steps.say: Start where the paper's estimate sits: each case infects 2.2 people. 100 cases become 220, then 484, and the bars climb steeply.
This average, counted in a population where nobody is immune yet, has a name: the basic reproductive number (R0). For Wuhan up to January 4, the paper estimates R0 at 2.2.
Lower R0 to 1.5. The outbreak still grows, just more slowly: each generation is 1.5 times the one before.
Now set R0 to exactly 1. Each case replaces itself once, so every bar is 100. The outbreak neither grows nor dies out.
That value of 1 is the epidemic threshold: the tipping point between growth and decline.
Drop R0 below 1, to 0.7. Now each generation is smaller than the last: 100, 70, 49 and so on. The outbreak fades.
Control measures don't change the virus. They cut how many people each case actually reaches. Back at R0 = 2.2, block 30% of infections.
Each case now infects about 1.54 people. That is still above 1, so the bars still climb. Slowing spread is not enough: control has to push this number below 1.

understand.explanation: The basic reproductive number (R0) is the average number of people one case infects when nobody around them is immune yet. Each new generation is roughly R0 times the size of the one before. Above 1 the generations keep getting bigger; at exactly 1, the epidemic threshold, they stay the same size; below 1 they shrink and the outbreak fades. Using the timing of the early Wuhan cases up to January 4, the paper estimated R0 at 2.2, but the uncertainty is wide (95% CI, 1.4 to 3.9). Control measures work by cutting how many people each case actually infects, and they aim to push that number below 1, as happened with SARS (R0 near 3), which was controlled by isolating patients. R0 is only an average: some people infect many others and some infect no one, and the paper warns that such super-spreading could appear as the epidemic goes on.
understand.quote: We estimated an R0 of approximately 2.2, meaning that on average each patient has been spreading infection to 2.2 other people. In general, an epidemic will increase as long as R0 is greater than 1, and control measures aim to reduce the reproductive number to less than 1.

connect.caption: This is the teaching model's rule, not an equation printed in the paper. R0 (the first slider) times the share of infections not blocked (the second slider) gives R, the number of people each case actually infects. Each generation is R times the one before, so after five steps generation 6 is 100 × R⁵. If R is above 1 that number grows; if R is below 1 it shrinks. The paper's estimate of R0 = 2.2 came from a fuller transmission model fitted to the early Wuhan cases.

concepts.recap: R0 is how many people one case infects on average when nobody is immune: above 1 each generation grows, below 1 the outbreak fades, so control measures aim to push the real number below 1.

concepts.title: Working out R0 from doubling time and serial interval
concepts.idea: If you know how fast cases grow and how far apart generations are, you can infer how many people each case infects: faster growth or longer gaps between generations both mean a larger R0.

predict.question: Suppose a later study found the gap between generations was nearer 4.5 days, not 7.5, while cases still grew at Wuhan's speed. What would happen to the R0 estimate?
options: It rises, because generations come faster
It falls, but stays above 1
It falls below 1, so the outbreak was really shrinking
It stays the same, because growth speed alone sets R0
why: Faster generations sound like faster spread. But the growth speed is fixed here, so with fewer days per generation, each case needs fewer infections to produce that same growth.
Right. At Wuhan's growth rate a 4.5-day gap gives about 1.5. A shorter gap means less multiplying per generation. But a growing epidemic always needs each case to infect more than one person.
A shorter gap does lower R0. But cases were still growing, and while growth is above zero the implied R0 stays above 1. The curve never drops below the tipping line.
Growth speed is only half the story. The same daily growth gives a different number per case depending on how many days one generation takes.

terms.means: A rule that builds each day's new cases from earlier cases, weighted by how long ago those earlier patients fell ill

model.title: How many people each case infects, from growth speed and the gap between generations
model.note: Teaching model: it assumes every new patient falls ill exactly one serial interval after the person who infected them, with no spread, so R0 = exp(growth rate × serial interval). The paper instead fitted a transmission model in which the serial interval varies from patient to patient (mean 7.5 days, SD 3.4). That model used a prior based on SARS and gave R0 = 2.2 (95% CI, 1.4 to 3.9). At Wuhan's values this simpler rule gives about 2.0. The 7.4-day doubling time, the 7.5-day serial interval and the 2.2 estimate are the paper's. Every other point on the curve is illustrative.

controls.label: Serial interval (gap between one patient and the next)

steps.say: This curve answers one question: how many people does each patient infect? Higher up means more people.
Left to right is how fast cases grow each day. This slider sets that speed, and the box shows how many days cases take to double.
This slider sets the gap between one patient falling ill and the person they infected falling ill. Watch the curve bend.
The dot is your outbreak. The flat line is the tipping point, where each case infects exactly one person.
This point marks the paper's own estimate for Wuhan.

explore.prompt: Two outbreaks can grow at the same speed yet differ in how many people each case infects. Use both sliders to build these two unusual outbreaks.

goals.text: Build a slow outbreak that is still very contagious: cases take at least 10 days to double, yet each case infects more than 2 people.
hints: A slow doubling means a small growth rate. What else can make each case infect more people?
Keep growth low enough for a 10-day doubling, then stretch the gap between generations.
Each case infects more than 2 when one generation takes longer than one doubling. So make the gap longer than the doubling time shown in the box.

goals.text: Now the reverse: a fast outbreak that is only mildly contagious. Cases double in under 5 days, yet each case infects fewer than 2 people.
hints: A fast doubling needs a high growth rate. What keeps each case's count of infections low?
Shrink the gap between generations, so the outbreak takes many quick, small steps.
Each case infects fewer than 2 when a new generation arrives before cases have had time to double. So make the gap shorter than the doubling time.

feedback.correct: Yes. With the growth speed fixed, a shorter gap leaves fewer days of growth inside each generation, so each case must have infected fewer people. That comes to about 1.5 at a 4.5-day gap. Because cases are still growing, R0 stays above 1.
feedback.incorrect: R0 is how much cases multiply over one generation. At the same daily growth, a shorter generation means less multiplying per generation, so R0 goes down. Any outbreak that is still growing keeps R0 above 1.

steps.say: Start at Wuhan-like growth of 0.10 per day, with generations only 2 days apart. Each case needs to infect only about 1.2 people. Small steps, taken often, add up quickly.
Keep the same growth but space generations 6 days apart. Cases now grow for more days between one generation and the next, so each case must have infected more people: about 1.8.
Keep the 6-day gap and double the growth rate. Faster growth over the same gap also means more infections per case: about 3.3.
That is the whole trick. R0 is how much cases multiply over one gap between generations. Growth speed times gap length sets it, so the dot always rides on this curve.
Now Wuhan. The paper found cases doubled about every 7.4 days, and each new patient fell ill about 7.5 days after the person who infected them.
So one generation takes about as long as one doubling. Each generation is about twice the size of the one before, which means each patient infected about 2 people.

The paper used a fuller method: a renewal equation that also lets the gap vary from patient to patient. It gave 2.2 (95% CI, 1.4 to 3.9). Two timing facts were enough, and nobody had to watch a single infection happen.

understand.explanation: The growth rate tells you how fast cases multiply each day. The serial interval tells you how many days one generation of cases takes. Put them together and you get how much cases multiply per generation, which is R0. So faster growth, or a longer gap between generations, both mean each case infected more people. The paper fitted a transmission model built on renewal equations to cases with onset from December 10 to January 4 that were not linked to the market. Using a serial interval estimated from just 6 pairs of cases, it got R0 = 2.2. The 95% confidence interval runs from 1.4 to 3.9, so the true value is uncertain. The paper stopped at January 4 because wider testing after that changed how many cases were caught.
understand.quote: In the epidemic curve up to January 4, 2020, the epidemic growth rate was 0.10 per day (95% CI, 0.050 to 0.16) and the doubling time was 7.4 days (95% CI, 4.2 to 14). Using the serial interval distribution above, we estimated that R0 was 2.2 (95% CI, 1.4 to 3.9).

check.task: Another virus grows at the paper's reported rate of 0.10 per day, but each of its cases infects about 3 people. Put the model in that state by finding how far apart its generations must be.
check.hint: Same growth, bigger R0: should generations be closer together or further apart? Set the growth rate first, then move only the other slider.
check.misconception: R0 depends only on how fast cases grow, so two viruses that grow equally fast must infect the same number of people per case.

connect.caption: The paper prints no formula, so this is the teaching model's rule. It assumes every generation is exactly T days apart. r (blue) is the daily growth rate and T (orange) is the serial interval. T_{d} is the doubling time, and R_{0} is how much cases multiply in one generation. In words: count how many doublings fit into one generation. For Wuhan, 7.5 ÷ 7.4 ≈ 1 doubling, so R0 ≈ 2. The paper's renewal-equation model also lets the gap vary from patient to patient, and it gave 2.2.

concepts.recap: Divide the serial interval by the doubling time to count doublings per generation: 7.5 ÷ 7.4 ≈ 1, so each Wuhan patient infected about 2 people (paper: 2.2).

sources.title: Early Transmission Dynamics in Wuhan, China, of Novel Coronavirus–Infected Pneumonia
